Azure Cloud-Native Platform Updates

Follow meaningful documentation updates across Microsoft's Azure cloud-native platform, spanning container orchestration and fleet management (AKS, AKS Automatic, Application Network, AKS Support, AKS Arc, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Fleet Manager), container registry (Azure Container Registry), application networking (Application Gateway for Containers), and Azure Linux. The tracker also summarizes the latest five AKS and Application Network releases.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.
  • Flatcar Container Linux node images are removed, affecting scaling operations.
  • The annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-pip-tags no longer overrides public IP tags.
🔑

Key Features

  • Identity bindings are now generally available.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 is available in preview.
  • Windows Server OS SKU migration to 2025 is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.
  • AKS no longer produces VHDs for Windows Server 2019 and version 23H2.
🔑

Key Features

  • Autoscaling for Virtual Machines node pools is now generally available.
  • Kubernetes patch versions 1.36.3, 1.35.7, and 1.34.10 are available.
  • On-Demand Monitor for node health checks is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • LocalDNS is enabled automatically for compatible cluster networking.
  • AKS rejects updates that remove IPv6 from dual-stack clusters.
  • Managed namespace creation rejects names starting with reserved prefixes.

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026: - Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools. - AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools. - Existing node pools won’t receive security patches. On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options: - Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade. - Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools. For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Ubuntu 20.04 has been replaced by newer supported versions, including Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04. We encourage you to transition to Ubuntu 22.04+ before the retirement date. Required action: If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with a Confidential VM (CVM) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.33+ where Ubuntu 24.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for CVM workloads. If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with Federal Information Process Standard (FIPS) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ where Ubuntu 22.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for FIPS workloads. To avoid service disruptions, scaling restrictions, and remain supported, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ by March 17, 2027. On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity. We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup. We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service. If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

On June 30, 2027, we'll retire Ubuntu 22.04 on Azure Kubernetes Service. To avoid disruptions, transition to Ubuntu 24.04 or later by that date. Newer supported versions include kernel updates and security improvements. Until June 30, 2027, you can continue to use Ubuntu 22.04 on AKS without disruption. If you don't migrate by June 30, 2027, you won't be able to create new node pools, AKS won't produce new node images, and you'll no longer receive security patches for existing node pools. On April 30, 2028 AKS will remove Ubuntu 22.04 node images and existing code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Migration Options: - Default Operating System SKU (OSSku): If you're using 'Ubuntu,' you'll automatically migrate to Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.35 or later. - Versioned OSSku: If you're using 'Ubuntu2204,' update your OSSku to 'Ubuntu' for Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or 'Ubuntu2404' for Kubernetes 1.32 or later. Read moreRead less
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters: - Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase) - Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready) After this change: - Metric names remain unchanged. - Aggregate pod counts remain available. - Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported. - The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting. During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement. You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow: - Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension. - Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension. Recommended action: - If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required. - If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics. Help and support If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Read moreRead less
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027. Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster. After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support. Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Read moreRead less
Azure Container Registry (ACR) implements Docker Content Trust (DCT), allowing image publishers to sign their images and image consumers to verify that the images they pull are signed. With advancements in technology, Docker Content Trust no longer meets the requirements of modern supply chain security for containers. As a result, Docker Content Trust will be deprecated and no longer available in ACR after March 31, 2028. If you currently use Docker Content Trust, you should transition to the Notary Project ecosystem, including their open-source supply chain tool, Notation. How does this affect me? - Starting September 30, 2025, customers will no longer be able to enable Docker Content Trust on Azure Container Registry. - Data stored in Azure Container Registry for signing and verifying signatures with Docker Content Trust will be permanently deleted on March 31, 2028. - Docker Content Trust function will be completely removed from Azure Container Registry on March 31, 2028. Required Action Start your transition to Notary Project today and enhance the security and trust of your container ecosystem. Use the following articles to get started. Signing: - Use AKV with self-signed certificates - Use AKV with CA-issued certificates - Sign in ADO pipelines - Sign in GitHub workflows Verification: - Verify in ADO pipelines - Verify in GitHub workflows - Verify on AKS

Read moreRead less
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS will be retired on November 30, 2025, please transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by that date. Azure Linux 2.0 has been replaced by the newer supported version Azure Linux 3.0. We encourage you to transition to Azure Linux 3.0 prior to the retirement date to experience the capabilities of Azure Linux 3.0 including kernel updates and security improvements. From now to November 30, 2025, you can continue to use Azure Linux 2.0 without disruption. On November 30, 2025, Azure Linux 2.0 will no longer be supported on AKS; AKS will no longer create new node pools, produce new node images, or provide security updates for Azure Linux 2.0 after that date. On March 31, 2026, Azure Linux 2.0 node images will be removed. This will cause scaling operations to fail. Customers can transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by taking one of the following actions: - If you’re currently using Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.32+. - Alternately, starting Kubernetes version 1.28+ you can perform an in-place node pool update from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3, enabling you to migrate existing node pools from Azure Linux 2.0 to 3.0 while remaining on the same k8s version. Your node pool will automatically reimage to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 node image. See documentation here. To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Linux 3.0 by November 30, 2025.

Unlike tools that operate only at the Kubernetes layer, Container Network Insights Agent can also gather **host-level network statistics** through its Linux Networking plugin. The agent can inspect NIC ring buffers, kernel packet counters, SoftIRQ distribution, and socket buffer utilization across your cluster nodes. This surfaces low-level issues such as packet drops, network bottlenecks, and hardware-level saturation that are otherwise difficult to diagnose in a Kubernetes environment.

                                            @@ -1,57 +1,64 @@-# Overview of Azure Linux Security | Microsoft Learn+# Azure Linux security overview | Microsoft Learn -Azure Linux is built with a secure-by-default baseline and layered protections across boot, runtime, and update workflows. This article covers the security model, key features, and recommendations for validating security settings on Azure Linux.+Azure Linux 4 ships with Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) enforcing its targeted policy, and with SSH, kernel, and network hardening defaults applied. Azure network security groups (NSGs) filter inbound traffic by default; a host firewall is available when your workload needs one. -Note+These guides cover general-purpose Azure Linux 4 virtual machines (VMs). Azure Container Linux (ACL) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is covered in the [Azure Container Linux documentation](azure-container-linux-overview). -Azure Linux 4.0 is now in **preview** and is strictly limited to evaluation and testing purposes. It's not suitable for production use.+## Default security configuration -## Security model+These defaults apply to the general-purpose Azure Linux 4 VM image. Provisioning and image customization can override them. -The following table summarizes the core security principles that guide the design of Azure Linux and how they are implemented across the platform:+| Protection | Default configuration | Guide |+| --- | --- | --- |+| Mandatory access control | SELinux runs in enforcing mode with the targeted policy. | [Configure SELinux security](security-enhanced-linux-security) |+| Kernel and eBPF | Address space layout randomization is enabled, kernel log and pointer access are restricted, and unprivileged eBPF is disabled. | [Inspect kernel hardening](kernel-hardening) and [Use eBPF](extended-berkeley-packet-filter) |+| Host network | No host firewall is installed. NSGs filter inbound traffic. IP forwarding, ICMP redirects, and source routing are disabled. | [Secure the host network](network-security) |+| Interactive access | On key-based deployments, SSH password authentication is disabled. Direct root sign-in is denied. SSH uses hardened session limits and SHA-2 message authentication codes. | [Manage identity and access](identity-and-access) |+| Guest disk encryption | The VM root isn't encrypted with Linux Unified Key Setup (LUKS). Guest-managed data-volume encryption requires configuration. Azure platform encryption is separate. | [Protect disks and data](disk-and-data-protection) |+| Cryptography | `DEFAULT` sets cryptographic defaults for applications that consume the system policy. Application overrides can change them. | [Use system cryptographic libraries](system-crypto) |+| Auditing and logs | `auditd` is enabled, but its default rule disables syscall and file-watch auditing. That coverage requires additional rules. The journal is persistent. | [Configure security logging and auditing](logging-and-auditing) |+| Packages | DNF verifies package signatures. Repository metadata signature checking isn't enabled. | [Manage security updates](manage-common-vulnerabilities-exposures) | -| Security principle | Implementation in Azure Linux |-| --- | --- |-| Secure by default | Minimal package set, key-only SSH authentication, firewalld enabled |-| Defense in depth | SELinux mandatory access control, network hardening |-| Least privilege | SELinux policies, kernel capability restrictions |+## Security defaults reference -## Core security features+Use this reference to find where a default is set and how to check it on a running VM. Vendor files under `/usr/lib` and package-owned files can be replaced by updates. Put local changes in the override location that each guide describes. -### Secure by default baseline+The defaults and checks in this table were verified on a newly deployed VM from the general-purpose Azure Linux 4 image, before any configuration changes. Provisioning options, extensions, and configuration management can change the results on your VM. -- **Hardened kernel**: With ASLR, stack canaries, and pointer restrictions.-- **Minimal package set**: Only essential packages for core operating system (OS) functionality. No legacy protocols, development tools, or non-essential daemons in the base image.-- **No external network connections by default**: firewalld denies all inbound traffic except SSH.-- **Key-only SSH authentication**: Password authentication is disabled.-- **Package integrity**: All packages and repository metadata are GPG-signed.+| Setting | Default | Set in | Check |+| --- | --- | --- | --- |+| SELinux mode and policy | `enforcing`, `targeted` | `/etc/selinux/config` | `sestatus` |+| Host firewall | Not installed. The `nftables` and `iptables-legacy` tools are installed, but no inbound filtering rules are loaded. | Not applicable | `rpm -q firewalld`, `sudo nft list ruleset`, and `sudo iptables -S` |+| Root SSH sign-in | `PermitRootLogin no` and `DenyUsers root` | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-permit-root-login.conf` and `30-azurelinux-cis.conf` | `sudo sshd -T`, then find `permitrootlogin` and `denyusers` |+| SSH password authentication | `PasswordAuthentication no` on key-based deployments | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf`, written at provisioning | `sudo sshd -T`, then find `passwordauthentication` |+| SSH session limits | `MaxAuthTries 4`, `LoginGraceTime 60`, `MaxStartups 10:30:60`, `ClientAliveInterval 180` | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/30-azurelinux-cis.conf` and `50-client-alive-interval.conf` | `sudo sshd -T` |+| SSH algorithms | System cryptographic policy, with message authentication codes limited to SHA-2 | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/40-azurelinux-crypto-policies.conf` and `30-azurelinux-cis.conf` | `sudo sshd -T`, then find `kexalgorithms`, `ciphers`, and `macs` |+| SSH pre-authentication banner | `/etc/issue.net` | `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/30-azurelinux-cis.conf` | `cat /etc/issue.net` |+| `sudo` session handling | Commands run in a pseudo-terminal and are logged to `/var/log/sudo.log` | `/etc/sudoers.d/10-azurelinux-cis` | `sudo cat /etc/sudoers.d/10-azurelinux-cis` |+| Password hashing | `YESCRYPT` | `/etc/login.defs` | `grep ENCRYPT_METHOD /etc/login.defs` |+| Kernel parameters | Full address space layout randomization, restricted kernel pointers and log, restricted `ptrace`, unprivileged eBPF disabled | `/usr/lib/sysctl.d/70-azurelinux-hardening.conf` and the kernel build | `sysctl kernel.randomize_va_space kernel.kptr_restrict kernel.yama.ptrace_scope kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled` |+| Network parameters | Forwarding, redirects, source routing, and IPv6 router advertisements disabled; reverse path filtering, SYN cookies, and martian logging enabled | `/usr/lib/sysctl.d/70-azurelinux-hardening.conf` | `sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra` |+| Temporary file systems | `/tmp` and `/dev/shm` are `tmpfs` mounted `nosuid,nodev` | systemd mount units | `findmnt /tmp` and `findmnt /dev/shm` |+| Cryptographic policy | `DEFAULT`, including hybrid post-quantum key exchange | `/etc/crypto-policies/config` | `update-crypto-policies --show` |+| Audit daemon | Enabled; the default rule disables syscall auditing | `/etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules` | `sudo auditctl -l` |+| Journal | Persistent | `/var/log/journal` | `journalctl --disk-usage` |+| Package signatures | `gpgcheck=1`, `repo_gpgcheck=0` | `/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` | `grep -h gpgcheck /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo` | -### Runtime protections+For CIS Benchmark and Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) status, see the [Azure Linux compliance overview](compliance-overview). -- **SELinux:** In Enforcing mode. Targeted policy with pre-labeled packages.-- **eBPF hardening**: Unprivileged BPF disabled, interpreter disabled in favor of JIT.+## Configure protection for your workload -### Network security+Workload configuration determines the required access, audit coverage, and application controls. Differences from image defaults can reflect provisioning or configuration management rather than an error. -- **firewalld**: Enabled by default with nftables backend.-- **Network sysctl hardening**: Strict reverse path filtering, ICMP redirects disabled, SYN cookies enabled.-- **IPv6**: Enabled with hardening settings applied.+- Allow only the network access and account privileges the workload needs.+- Configure audit rules and retention for the required security events.+- Confirm that application processes and cryptographic settings use the intended protections.+- Apply updates and confirm that affected workloads run the updated code. -### Identity and access+Azure network security groups (NSGs), managed disk encryption, and Azure role assignments remain separate from guest configuration. Review both layers. For example, allowing a port in the guest doesn't override an NSG, and a managed identity grants access to Azure resources rather than an operating system sign-in. -- **SSSD/realmd**: Available from the Azure Linux repositories for hybrid identity scenarios with Active Directory and LDAP.+## Change security defaults deliberately -### Cryptography+Changes to security defaults require a documented workload requirement or approved baseline. Weaker settings can expose the workload; stricter settings can affect compatibility or performance. -- **FIPS 140-3**: Validated cryptographic modules with a simple enablement mechanism.-- **Post-quantum cryptography**: ML-KEM hybrid key exchange support.-- **System crypto libraries**: Applications can use OS-level crypto.--### Logging, auditing, and monitoring--- **auditd**: enabled by default; rule profiles ship under /usr/share/audit-rules/ and can be activated by copying the profile you need into /etc/audit/rules.d/.-- **journald**: Persistent storage with structured JSON output.--### Vulnerability scanning integrations--Azure Linux supports integration with common vulnerability scanning and security tooling. For a list of supported tools, see [Azure Linux partner solutions](ecosystem-support).+Production rollout requires representative nonproduction testing and a rollback plan. See [Apply security baselines safely](compliance-overview#apply-security-baselines-safely) for approval and recovery requirements.

You can have multiple `NodePools` that point to the same `AKSNodeClass`, allowing you to share common Azure configurations across different node pools. +## Kubernetes and node image versions++NAP allows you to control the Kubernetes and node image versions by using the `spec.versions` field in the `AKSNodeClass`. If you omit `spec.versions`, the node Kubernetes version follows the observed AKS control-plane version, and NAP automatically resolves compatible node images. When the control-plane version increases, NAP considers the nodes as `Drifted`, marks images as not ready, and resolves images for the new Kubernetes version. NAP doesn't currently automatically downgrade node Kubernetes versions.++For an up-to-date list of supported Kubernetes versions and node image versions, see the [AKS Release Tracker](https://releases.aks.azure.com/).++### Pin Kubernetes version++Set `spec.versions.kubernetesVersion` to pin the node Kubernetes version. Specify the full `major.minor.patch` version. AKS supports the version, and it's compatible with the control plane: it has the same major version, can't have a higher minor version, and can't be more than three minor versions behind. If the node and control plane use the same minor version, the node patch version can't be higher than the control-plane patch version. An invalid format, incompatible version, or unsupported target keeps the Kubernetes version condition false, so the `AKSNodeClass` isn't ready for provisioning.++### Pin node image version++Set `spec.versions.nodeImageVersion` to pin a node image version suffix. This value is the suffix after `/versions/` in an image ID, not a full image ID or an arbitrary value. The requested suffix must be present in the `AKSNodeClass` status as a currently resolved image, the latest image version, or a recently used image version. A recently used image version must be paired with its recorded Kubernetes version. The Kubernetes version and image version must be specified together: `nodeImageVersion` requires `kubernetesVersion`. If you change the Kubernetes version while pinning a current or latest image version, that combination must also be a recently used Kubernetes and image version pair.++Pinning an image version prevents automatic image roll-forward. To resume automatic image selection, remove `nodeImageVersion`; you can keep `kubernetesVersion` pinned if needed. The following example shows both fields. Replace the values with a supported Kubernetes version and an eligible image version suffix for your `AKSNodeClass`:++```yaml+spec:+  versions:+    kubernetesVersion: "1.34.0"+    nodeImageVersion: "2026.09.23"+```+ Important  Changing a setting on an existing `AKSNodeClass` doesn't reconfigure running nodes in place. NAP marks the nodes provisioned from the previous configuration as *drifted* and replaces them, subject to the disruption controls on the referencing `NodePool` resources. The `tags` field is the only exception, because tag changes apply to existing Azure resources without replacing the node. To learn more, see [Drift](node-auto-provisioning-disruption#drift) and [Disruption budgets](node-auto-provisioning-disruption#disruption-budgets).                                                                                                                                                                       @@ -43,6 +43,10 @@ For .NET, identity bindings support is available exclusively in **Azure.Identity  ## Frequently asked questions (FAQs) +### How does my application locate the projected token and CA certificate files?++The workload identity webhook injects `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE` for the token file path and `AZURE_KUBERNETES_CA_FILE` for the CA certificate file path. Read these environment variables instead of hard-coding paths or the injected volume name. `WorkloadIdentityCredential` configured for identity binding mode reads them for you. For more information, see [Locate the projected service account token](identity-bindings#locate-the-projected-service-account-token).+ ### Is identity sameness (namespace and service account sameness) required across clusters using the same UAMI?  No. Identity bindings don't require namespace/service account sameness. It's up to the cluster operator to explicitly authorize the namespaces and service accounts inside each cluster that are allowed to use the managed identity through role-based access control (RBAC).@@ -74,6 +78,28 @@ There's no automatic garbage collection of the FIC today when the last identity  Previously, workload identity required egress to `login.microsoftonline.com` so workloads could exchange service account tokens for Microsoft Entra access tokens. With identity bindings, token exchange requests route through a cluster-specific identity binding proxy operated by AKS. Direct egress to `login.microsoftonline.com` for token exchange isn't required. +### Why do my pods fail with `AADSTS700211` after I create the first identity binding on a cluster?++When you create the first identity binding on a cluster, AKS updates the workload identity webhook (`azure-wi-webhook-controller-manager` in the `kube-system` namespace) to support identity bindings. Until the updated webhook pods are running, the previous webhook mutates new pods. Those pods don't get the identity binding configuration and fall back to standard workload identity token exchange, which fails with `AADSTS700211` and names your cluster's OIDC issuer.++If your system node pool doesn't have enough spare CPU for an additional webhook pod, the new webhook pod stays in the `Pending` state and the update doesn't complete. The identity binding still shows a `Succeeded` provisioning state, because it doesn't track the webhook update.++To check the webhook pods and their events, run the following command:++```bash+kubectl describe pods --namespace kube-system --selector azure-workload-identity.io/system=true+```++If a pod is `Pending` and its events show `Insufficient cpu`, [scale your node pool](scale-cluster) or free up CPU on your system nodes. After the new webhook pods are running, delete and recreate your workload pods so the updated webhook mutates them.++### What happens if I delete and recreate a UAMI that identity bindings use?++A recreated UAMI gets a new client ID and principal ID. Existing identity bindings stay tied to the deleted identity, and updating them fails with a `ManagedIdentityRecreated` error. To use the new identity:++1. Delete and recreate each identity binding that references the UAMI. If another resource, such as a fleet, manages the binding, remove and reapply it through that resource.+2. Update your RBAC objects and service account annotations to the new client ID, and then restart your pods.+3. Assign Azure roles to the new principal ID.+ ### What limitations exist for identity bindings?  Identity bindings aren't yet supported on clusters configured with [API server virtual network integration](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration).

The `kubectl describe pods` command shows repeated `FailedMount` events that have the `Aborted` status code instead of the `Internal` code that mount errors usually have:++```output+Events:+  Type     Reason       Age                   From     Message+  ----     ------       ----                  ----     -------+  Warning  FailedMount  22s (x10 over 4m32s)  kubelet  MountVolume.MountDevice failed for volume "<pv-name>" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given Volume ID <volume-handle> already exists+```++The `<volume-handle>` value is the `volumeHandle` field of the PersistentVolume (PV).++### Cause++The Azure Files CSI driver allows only one operation at a time for each volume on a node. While the driver stages (mounts) or unstages a volume, it holds a lock for that volume. Kubelet retries failed or slow calls. If a retry reaches the driver while the first operation still holds the lock, the driver rejects the retry with the "An operation with the given Volume ID already exists" message.++The message itself doesn't identify the problem. It means that an earlier operation for the same volume on the same node didn't finish. The most common reasons are:++- **A slow or stuck mount operation.** The first mount takes longer than kubelet waits for a response. Examples are a stale or hung SMB connection to the storage account, intermittent network problems between the node and the storage account, or multiple leftover `cifs` mounts of the same share on the node.+- **A slow ownership change on an NFS share.** If the pod sets `fsGroup`, Kubernetes recursively changes ownership and permissions of the volume contents. On a share that has a large number of files, this operation can take a long time.+- **Two PVs that use the same `volumeHandle` on the same node.** Kubelet treats all PVs that have the same `volumeHandle` as one volume. Both pods share a single mount, so one pod might write to a different share than the one that its PV references.++### Troubleshooting++#### Step 1: Check whether the mount is still in progress or already exists++Use the `kubectl debug` command to open a shell on the node that hosts the pod, and then check for existing SMB mounts and connections:++```bash+kubectl debug node/<node-name> -it --image=mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/base/core:3.0 --profile=sysadmin -- chroot /host+```++```bash+mount | grep "type cifs"+ss -t | grep microsoft-ds+```++If the same share appears more than once, or if connections to the storage account are stuck, the node has a stale or duplicate mount.++#### Step 2: Check for duplicate volume handles++List the volume handle of every PV, and look for duplicate values:++```bash+kubectl get pv -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.spec.csi.driver=="file.csi.azure.com")]}{.spec.csi.volumeHandle}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' | sort+```++Each PV must have a unique `volumeHandle` value.++#### Step 3: Check the CSI driver logs on the node++Find the `csi-azurefile-node` pod that runs on the affected node, and look for the lock message and the original mount operation:++```bash+kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=csi-azurefile-node -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>+kubectl logs -n kube-system <csi-azurefile-node-pod-name> -c azurefile | grep -E "already exists|NodeStageVolume|timed out"+```++### Solution++1. If the operation is still running, wait for it to finish. Kubelet retries automatically, and the pod starts after the first operation completes.+2. If the operation doesn't finish, or the node has stale or duplicate mounts, delete the pod so that it's re-created. Then restart the CSI node pod on the same node:++    ```bash+    kubectl delete pod -n kube-system <csi-azurefile-node-pod-name>+    ```+3. If the problem persists or occurs again, [cordon and drain](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/) the node, and then let the pod be scheduled on a different node or on the same node after it's uncordoned. As a last resort, restart or reimage the node.+4. If two PVs have the same `volumeHandle`, give each PV a unique value. For a statically provisioned volume, use the `<resource-group>#<storage-account>#<file-share>` format:++    ```yaml+    csi:+      driver: file.csi.azure.com+      volumeHandle: <resource-group>#<storage-account>#<file-share>+    ```++    The `volumeHandle` field of an existing PV can't be changed. Delete and re-create the PV and PVC, and then re-create the pods.+5. If the volume is an NFS share that has many files and the pod sets `fsGroup`, set `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` or `None` in the pod's `securityContext` to skip the recursive ownership change.+ ## `AuthorizationFailed` error during Azure Files share provisioning  ### Symptoms

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      @@ -248,6 +248,27 @@ The `--gpu-instance-profile` feature remains available for configuration of your  All three single-strategy paths expose partitions as `nvidia.com/gpu` when configured on an NVIDIA GPU node pool. The resource name alone doesn't identify the partition size or whether AKS manages the plugin. +Important++[NVIDIA Container Toolkit 1.20.1](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/releases/tag/v1.20.1) and later won't start a container that sets `NVIDIA_MIG_CONFIG_DEVICES` or `NVIDIA_MIG_MONITOR_DEVICES` unless the container has the `SYS_ADMIN` capability. Self-managed device plugin and GPU feature discovery containers usually set one of these variables when they run with a MIG strategy. Without the capability, they fail with this error:++```output+invalid MIG capability request: cannot set NVIDIA_MIG_CONFIG_DEVICES or NVIDIA_MIG_MONITOR_DEVICES in a non-privileged container+```++The NVIDIA device plugin Helm chart adds `SYS_ADMIN` for you, unless you override `securityContext` in your values. If you override it, or you deploy your own manifest, add the capability yourself. Kubernetes doesn't allow `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` on a container that has `SYS_ADMIN`, so remove that setting or set it to `true`. You don't need `privileged: true`:++```yaml+securityContext:+  allowPrivilegeEscalation: true+  capabilities:+    add: ["SYS_ADMIN"]+```++For more information, see [Configure a security context for a pod or container](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/).++If AKS manages the device plugin for you, there's nothing to change. The managed plugin runs as a systemd service on the node, so this check doesn't apply to it.+ ### Validate the MIG profiles configuration  - Supply exactly one profile value to `--gpu-mig-profiles` for `Single`, not repeated entries to specify a partition count.

The sandbox is the isolation boundary for all containers and steps in a task run.++You're responsible for keeping secrets out of your images. Use a [`.dockerignore` file](https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/context/#dockerignore-files) at the root of the Docker build context to exclude sensitive files such as private keys. `az acr build` applies ignore rules before uploading a local directory. For Git sources, Docker applies the rules during the image build.+ ## Image platforms  By default, Azure Container Registry tasks build images for the Linux OS and the AMD64 architecture. Specify the `--platform` tag to build Windows images or Linux images for other architectures. Specify the OS and optionally a supported architecture in *OS/architecture* format (for example, `--platform Linux/arm`). For ARM architectures, optionally specify a variant in *OS/architecture/variant* format (for example, `--platform Linux/arm64/v8`).

For example, choose times when teams are available to monitor or when user traffic is at its lowest.  Fleet Manager provides scheduled start gates that platform administrators can use to delay the progression of an update run until a specified day and time. For example, you can place a scheduled start gate before the production stage of an update strategy. This gate ensures that production clusters don't begin updating until the scheduled time, even if earlier stages complete ahead of schedule.  This article covers how to define scheduled start gates in update strategies, and how they complete during update run execution. -Important--Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager preview features are available on a self-service, opt-in basis.
